text: When you feed text into a large language model, the system first chops those words into smaller
chunks called tokens.
Each token is then assigned a unique token ID.
But since that ID is just a random number, how does the AI actually know what the underlying
word means?
These four student ID cards illustrate a limitation of identifiers.
Numbers like 1024 or 2048 identify exactly who a student is, but describe nothing about them.
The ID grants access, but fails to tell us if that person is funny, plays hockey, or steals
fries at lunch.
To an AI, a token ID is essentially just a catalog number.
A completely different system is required to describe a token's actual characteristics
and capture its meaning.
We can describe characteristics using numbers by looking at a taste test comparing Coke and
coffee.
Here, we rate them on six specific characteristics using a scale from 0 to 10.
Looking at the extremes in the data, Coke scores a 9 in sweet and a 10 in fizz, while
coffee scores a 9 in bitter and an 8 in caffeine.
These numbers create a distinct mathematical profile for each drink.
In data science, this entire row of numbers is called a vector.
Each specific position across the top, like sweet or bitter, is a dimension, and the specific
number sitting in that spot is its value.
Now, we run into a problem.
If we add a third drink, Pepsi, to our taste test, it scores exactly the same as Coke
on all six of our original dimensions.
Take a moment and consider.
If our six numbers are identical, how can we mathematically tell Coke and Pepsi apart?
The solution is to add a seventh dimension, citrus.
Pepsi scores a 10 here, while Coke scores a 1.
Adding this new column allows the numerical profile to capture a subtle difference the
original six missed.
When basic numbers match, adding a new dimension separates similar meanings.
This math allows us to differentiate highly similar concepts.
Artificial intelligence uses this exact same concept to understand text.
A row of numbers represents an exhaustive list of characteristics.
This chart compares a human taste test directly to AI token mechanics.
While our taste test only mapped three specific drinks to rows,
an AI creates a row for every single token in its entire vocabulary.
And the AI doesn't stop at seven dimensions.
It typically utilizes thousands of separate dimensions to capture the deep
complexity of human language.
Instead of simple 0 to 10 ratings, the AI learns highly specific positive and
negative decimal numbers during its training phase.
Unlike our taste test, AI dimensions do not have human labels like sweetness or
fizz.
The values capture hidden patterns and how words are used alongside one another.
These unlabeled values work together to represent meaning.
In AI, this complete row of numbers is called an embedding.
This diagram takes us inside a real model to see how this works in practice,
starting with a user typing the word cat into a prompt.
The word cat is assigned token ID 4719.
The AI uses this ID purely as an address to locate its specific row inside
a massive database called an embedding table.
The columns labeled D1, D2, and so on represent the thousands of dimensions.
Each cell contains a learned value, which in AI terminology is called a parameter.
This single complete row of parameters is the token's embedding,
its unique mathematical definition based on its relationship to every other token.
Every piece of text the model processes receives this treatment.
Word fragments like UN, BELIE, and VABLE each have their own unique token IDs and
dedicated rows of numbers in the table.
AI uses these numbers to work with meaning, and
those numbers are what help AI mathematically recognize similarities and
differences in language.
